parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys goes to White Hall to obtain a privy seal for cutting the King's timber for the navy and speaks with the Lord Privy Seal. At the Exchange, he encounters further bad news about a Frenchman captured and released by a Dutch man-of-war and seven other large ships off the North Foreland. He reflects that it is a strange attempt for the Dutch to come so close to England, but notes that the easterly wind will blow them away while preventing reinforcements from Portsmouth. He prays for God to preserve England from the Dutch and to pardon the English for treating them as a contemptible enemy in discourse. He then goes home for dinner with Mr. Hollyard, works at the office until after 11 at night, and returns home for supper and bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The Dutch fleet is a serious threat that has been underestimated, though the wind may drive them away while also isolating England.

They referred the business to a meeting of Mr. Sherwin and others to settle, but the narrator found it strange to sit in Committee with his hat on while Mr. Sherwin stood bare as a clerk, though he thanked God he did not think himself the better man for it. Thence he went with Creed to the 'Change and Coffee-house, and home to a brave dinner of pheasants, very merry about Povy's folly. He then went to the office and sat very late, visited Sir W. Batten where he was mighty great, returned to the office again until late, and finally went home to sort his books before bed as the weather grew warm and he hoped the frost would break.

parsed.narrative.summary: Samuel Pepys rose at five, traveled to White Hall and Chelsea fearing obstacles to his Tangier Privy Seal petition, but was pleasantly surprised when the Lord Privy Seal passed it without comment and treated him civilly. After joyfully returning to London to deliver the seal and attend a dinner at Trinity House and observe poison experiments at Gresham College, he met with Mr. Povy, who discouraged him about obtaining money, warning that it would be difficult and suspecting Backewell intended to force the matter upon himself. This plunged Pepys into a cruel melancholy at the thought of losing what he had nearly secured, though he retained some hope for the next day and consulted with Creed about approaching Lord Ashly. Meeting Mr. Warren further dampened his hopes of securing a protection, but he accepted that his troubles would either resolve or reach their worst within a day or two, before retiring early with a headache.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He concluded that Mr. Povy was a most cunning fellow.

Carteret and Secretary Morris, staying with Mr. Hunt at the Secretary's chamber until noon when the recognizances were entered. He returned home vexed to have been kept from his office all morning, then dined and worked late into the night at the office. Throughout the day he heard news of the two fleets engaged and felt concernment for the Duke, particularly for Lord Sandwich and Mr. Coventry. On Sunday he completed his accounts, finding himself worth £1400, more than ever before, and settled his Tangier accounts with great joy. He also recorded a discourse with Mr. Howell about Paymaster J. Fenn's practices for future remembrance, and learned the fleet was pursuing the Dutch.

Carteret and the Board, where they discussed unreliable news about the fleet, he returned to the office and felt great vexation that the Controller had not rectified the King's accounts. He wrote letters all afternoon, then traveled by coach to Sir Ph. Warwick regarding Tangier business to obtain money, and visited Lady Sandwich, who was in good temper despite expecting news of her husband. She informed him that Lord Rochester was no longer hoping to marry Mrs. Mallett and that the King might give leave to Lord Hinchingbroke to pursue her. He returned home by coach, stopped briefly at his office, and went to bed before midnight.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He did not give much belief to the news that the fleet was well and had beaten the Dutch.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went to White Hall with Sir J. Minnes to the Committee of Tangier, where the Lord Treasurer promised £15,000, which Pepys noted would be short. Pepys walked to Woolwich via Greenwich to arrange his wife's summer there, agreeing it would be good for both, then returned weary, worked until midnight, and observed with sadness the plague increasing and a house shut up in the street.

Lady Batten invited the group to dine to vex the niggardly Sir W. Doyly, and they returned home full of mirth. At Greenwich, Lord Rutherford and Creed delivered orders for over £7000 for Tangier, which the subject paid with tallys, then left without lingering. He went by water to Woolwich to play backgammon with his wife before bed.
canon.narrative.meaning: Life is a game where one may mend bad fortune by wiser play.

After tea with Mr. Pierce and travel by water to London, he hears troubling news at the 'Change that the plague has increased again, though he hopes the recent frosts will reverse the trend. He lunches with Sheriff Hooker, then meets Captain Cocke at the Pope's Head Tavern, where Cocke signs a bill for L2,000, gladdening him, and later advises with Sir W. Warren about securing L100 and arranging insurance for goods under convoy. They attempt to get the Duke of Albemarle's advice at the Cockepitt but are refused without the Duke of York's knowledge, so they return home, where he finds his wife well but worries that their parish has the highest plague count in the city. He concludes the day by finalizing insurance arrangements with Lord Bruncker and going to bed with his mind in great rest.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He concludes that he can rest his mind despite the troubling plague news.

parsed.narrative.summary: Spent the morning at the office and dined with colleagues at Captain Cocke's on mostly unroasted beef and fowl they prepared themselves, in merry company including Mr. Evelyn. The afternoon was pleasant until night when he returned to the office to write letters, then went home with his head full of business and trouble over his neglected accounts, making an oath to abstain from wine until his accounts were cleared. That evening the sister of his servant boy, Daniel, provided him a supper of little birds, and after they ate together alone he enjoyed kisses from her, noting she is a pretty woman. Earlier in the day he was visited by Mrs. Burrows, the widow of his acquaintance Lieutenant Burrows, a pretty and modest woman with whom he shared a kiss or two.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He realized he needed to rectify his neglected accounts, prompting him to swear off wine until they were cleared.
